title: How to Use Mechanics Instruction that Sticks When Teaching Remotely oughts-from-the-author-doug-stark
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Guest author Doug Stark explains how he plans to adapt Mechanics Instruction That Sticks (MITS) for remote and hybrid teaching, drawing on lessons from his district's improvised spring 2020 transition to online learning. He describes the "weekly work" model he used when his district lacked reliable tech access — a single Google document laying out the week's reading and writing tasks, paired with short cell-phone-recorded instructional videos — and explains how he intends to fold brief MITS warm-ups and guided notes into that same weekly structure this fall. Stark is candid that online delivery of the mechanics warm-ups has real limitations, but argues the format still preserves what matters most: direct instruction on conventions, followed by application to students' actual writing through self- and peer-editing. He closes with his central belief that students cannot become effective editors without first being given explicit knowledge of the rules.
points: Stark's spring 2020 fallback for students without reliable internet access was a single weekly Google document plus short cell-phone-recorded video lessons, with paper copies for offline students.
His plan for MITS this fall folds brief guided-notes or warm-up lessons into that same weekly structure, recorded step-by-step in short instructional videos.
He explicitly names the limitations of online delivery for the warm-ups while arguing the core sequence — direct instruction, then application to real writing — still transfers.
Stark's stated core belief is that direct instruction in conventions is a precondition for effective self- and peer-editing, not an optional add-on.
quotes: That was my first experience with online instruction, and I thought it went reasonably well considering how little time I had to adapt, but I was lucky.
Last spring, my school district was not prepared for a transition to online schooling, and we had a significant number of students who lacked access to technology and/or internet.
I then recorded short, instructional videos on my cell phone and posted links to them on the Google document. This made it quite simple for students to follow along with my lesson plans.
Obviously, using the warm-ups online will have its limitations, but the warm-ups do give you a chance to include some direct instruction on conventions within your curriculum.
I hold one central belief about teaching writing conventions: at some point, you have to include some direct instruction.
Students learn how to become better writers by writing, editing/revising, and rewriting, but they do not become effective editors unless they hold some core knowledge about the rules.
